# Session 6: Protein Structure

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to:

- describe the four levels of protein structure, using hemoglobin, and
  name the computational task that belongs to each;
- represent a structure as coordinates, as a distance map and as a
  contact map, and explain what each makes easy to see;
- explain the difference between a sequence alignment and a structure
  alignment, and why structure is often more conserved than sequence;
- interpret RMSD and TM-score, and explain at a conceptual level how
  DALI and Foldseek compare structures;
- explain why a single PDB entry is not necessarily "the" structure of a
  protein;
- state secondary-structure prediction as a supervised learning problem:
  what goes in, what comes out.

The question for today: **what information about a protein is contained
in its sequence, what becomes visible only in 3D, and how can computers
connect the two?** Sessions 3–5 worked with sequences: retrieving them,
aligning them, searching for families. In Session 3 you found structures
as *database records* (a PDB entry, an AlphaFold model). Today the
structure itself becomes the data: coordinates that can be turned into
distances, secondary structure, domains and interfaces, and compared
with other structures. The course's globin thread continues: in Session
3 you looked up *HBB*'s identifiers, in Session 4 you aligned globin
sequences, in Session 5 you searched for the globin family; today you
compare globin structures.

## Sequence becomes structure {#sec-s06-levels}

### Four levels, four computational tasks

A protein starts as a **polypeptide chain**, a linear polymer of amino
acids, which folds into a 3D shape. Structural biology describes the
result at four levels, and each level has its own computational problem
in this course:

| Level | What it is | Computational task | Where in the course |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | the amino-acid sequence | alignment, BLAST, profiles | Sessions 3–5 |
| **Secondary** | local backbone shapes: α-helix, β-strand, coil | prediction from sequence | Sessions 7–11 |
| **Tertiary** | the 3D fold of one chain | structure comparison, prediction | today; Session 12 |
| **Quaternary** | several chains packed together | interfaces, complexes | today; Session 12 |

- An **α-helix** is a coil held together by hydrogen bonds between the
  backbone N-H and C=O groups of residues four apart; a **β-sheet** is
  built from extended **β-strands** hydrogen-bonded edge to edge.
  Everything else is called **coil**. Programs such as DSSP assign these
  labels from the coordinates of a solved structure.
- The tertiary fold is held together mainly by the **hydrophobic
  effect** (non-polar side chains bury themselves away from water), plus
  hydrogen bonds, electrostatic interactions and van der Waals contacts.
- Many proteins work as a single chain; others assemble into complexes
  of two to hundreds of chains.

### Hemoglobin: all four levels in one protein

Hemoglobin is a **heterotetramer**: two α-globin chains (141 residues)
and two β-globin chains (146 residues; β-globin is *HBB*, this course's
running example since Session 3), each folded on its own and each
carrying an oxygen-binding heme group. The notebook computes with
PyMOL's secondary-structure algorithm (`dss`) that one β chain is **118
of 146 residues (80.8%) α-helix and 0% β-strand**; the PDB entry's own
annotation, which Session 7 uses, gives 117 helical residues. (Two
methods that differ only in where exactly a helix ends.)

![PDB entry `2HHB`, human deoxyhemoglobin: two α chains (blue/cyan),
two β chains (salmon/pink), four heme iron atoms (orange spheres).
Rendered from the real structure with PyMOL.](figs/session06-hemoglobin-tetramer.png){width=85%}

### Does the sequence determine the structure?

In the 1950s and 60s Christian Anfinsen showed that ribonuclease, unfolded
in the test tube, refolds into its active shape on its own once the
denaturant is removed. For many small globular proteins, then, the
sequence contains enough information to specify the native fold under
the right conditions. This is the principle that makes structure
prediction possible at all. It is not a law for every protein: some
proteins need chaperones to fold efficiently, many need a ligand,
cofactor or binding partner, some switch between alternative states
(hemoglobin itself, below), and **intrinsically disordered** regions
have no single fold.

Two kinds of interaction build a fold. **Local** interactions, between
residues close in sequence, form secondary structure: the hydrogen bonds
of an α-helix connect residues $i$ and $i+4$. **Long-range**
interactions, between residues far apart in sequence but close in space,
pack the helices and strands into a tertiary structure. Local structure
can be partly guessed from a short window of sequence (Session 7);
long-range structure cannot, which is why tertiary-structure prediction
is so much harder.

### A structure as a matrix: distance and contact maps

A structure file is a list of atomic coordinates. A useful alternative
representation is the distance between every pair of residues: for a
chain of $L$ residues, an $L \times L$ **distance map**. Thresholding it
gives a **contact map**: 1 where two residues are close (here, Cβ atoms
within 8 Å), 0 elsewhere. Unlike coordinates, both stay the same however
the protein is rotated or moved, so two structures can be compared
without first superimposing them.

![Three representations of β-globin (2HHB, chain B). Left: the 3D
structure, coloured from the N-terminus (blue) to the C-terminus (red).
Middle: the distance map. Right: the contact map, with the eight
α-helices of the PDB file as red bars. The band along the diagonal is
each helix in contact with itself (local interactions); the
off-diagonal stripes are helices packed against each other (long-range
interactions).](figs/session06-hbb-distance-map.png){width=100%}

This representation returns twice later in the course. An $L \times L$
map looks like an image, which is why image-processing networks (CNNs,
Session 10) turned out to be good at predicting contacts; and
coevolution, contact prediction and AlphaFold's "pair representation"
(Session 12) all work on residue-pair information like this.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Representations

The same protein can be represented as a sequence, a profile (Session 5),
a set of coordinates, a distance or contact map, or a learned embedding
(Session 11). The choice of representation determines which patterns are
easy to see, and later in the course, which patterns a model can easily
learn.
:::

### Looking at structures: PyMOL

[PyMOL](https://pymol.org/) is, with ChimeraX, one of the two most
widely used molecular viewers, and free in its open-source version. It
loads a structure directly from the PDB and shows it as **cartoon**
(secondary structure as ribbons and arrows, as in the figures above),
**sticks** (every bond, useful for a side chain or ligand) or **spheres**
(every atom, useful for packing), and measures distances and angles
directly from the coordinates. Today's lab uses it hands-on; the notebook
drives the same program from Python, without a window, so that its
figures and measurements are reproducible.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Protein structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure) and [Anfinsen's dogma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anfinsen%27s_dogma)
- RCSB [PDB-101](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/) — short, illustrated explainers on structure and specific proteins, aimed at newcomers

## Comparing proteins in 3D {#sec-s06-compare}

### Sequence alignment versus structure alignment

Session 4 defined an alignment as a hypothesis about which residues
correspond. A **sequence alignment** decides this from the sequences
alone, using substitution scores. A **structure alignment** decides it
from the 3D coordinates: which residues occupy the same position in the
two folds. The notebook compares β-globin with five proteins, from a
close paralog to an unrelated fold, both ways:

| Compared with β-globin | Sequence identity\* | Sequence-only score (shuffled max) | Residue pairs agreeing | TM-score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| α-globin (human, 2HHB) | 43% | 288 (43) | 95% | 0.88 |
| myoglobin (human, 3RGK) | 25% | 111 (46) | 97% | 0.91 |
| neuroglobin (human, 1OJ6) | 22% | 89 (41) | 66% | 0.82 |
| truncated hemoglobin N (*M. tuberculosis*, 1IDR) | 16% | 28 (49) | 0% | 0.57 |
| GFP (jellyfish, 1EMA) | 6% | 25 (50) | — | 0.33 |

\*Identity over the structurally aligned residues. "Sequence-only
score" is the best Smith–Waterman alignment with BLOSUM62; in brackets,
the highest score among 200 alignments against shuffled versions of the
same sequence. "Residue pairs agreeing" is the fraction of structurally
aligned pairs that the sequence alignment also pairs up. TM-scores are
normalized by the length of β-globin.

Read it from top to bottom. For α-globin and myoglobin the sequence
alignment has a strong signal and pairs up almost exactly the same
residues as the structure alignment. (Session 5 showed that BLAST, with
default settings, nevertheless missed myoglobin: a heuristic search can
skip an alignment that an exhaustive one finds.) For neuroglobin the
sequence signal is still clear, but a third of the pairs are wrong: the
gaps are in the wrong places. For the bacterial truncated hemoglobin the
sequence alignment does no better than shuffled sequences, and pairs up
none of the right residues, yet the structure alignment still finds a
shared globin fold over more than 100 residues. This is the central
lesson: **structure is more conserved than sequence.** When sequence
evidence fades, structure can still reveal a relationship.

### Measuring structural similarity: RMSD and TM-score

**RMSD** (root-mean-square deviation) is the most direct measure: after
optimally superimposing two structures, the root-mean-square distance
between corresponding atoms. It is simple, but it grows with protein
length, and one badly placed loop can inflate it even when the rest of
the fold matches. The **TM-score** weights each residue pair by how close
it is, so that small deviations count fully and large ones hardly at
all, and normalizes by protein length. It runs from 0 to 1 (identical).
Unrelated proteins typically score around 0.2–0.3, and scores above
about 0.5 usually mean the same overall fold. This is a rule of thumb,
not a law: the truncated hemoglobin above (0.57) and GFP (0.33) are
clear cases, but scores in between need other evidence.

### DALI: comparing distance maps

If two proteins have the same fold, their distance maps should look
alike, even when their sequences do not. **DALI** (Holm & Sander, 1993)
compares structures this way: rather than superimposing coordinates, it
looks for residue correspondences that make the patterns of
intramolecular distances agree.

![Distance maps of β-globin, human myoglobin and GFP. The first two are
almost indistinguishable although only a quarter of their residues are
identical; GFP's β-barrel gives a completely different pattern.](figs/session06-distance-maps-compared.png){width=100%}

The analogy with sequence alignment is direct:

- sequence alignment compares residues along two sequences;
- DALI compares patterns of residue–residue geometry.

DALI and **TM-align** (Zhang & Skolnick, 2005), which finds the
superposition that maximizes the TM-score, are accurate and still used
for careful pairwise comparisons, but they are far too slow to search
hundreds of millions of structures.

### Foldseek: structure search at sequence-search speed

Session 5 ended with MMseqs2, which searches billions of sequences.
**Foldseek** (van Kempen, Steinegger et al., 2024), from the same group,
does the same for structures:

| | Search tool | Searches with |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence (Session 5) | BLAST, MMseqs2 | the amino-acid sequence |
| Structure (today) | Foldseek | a "structural sequence" |

Its key idea is a change of representation. For each residue, Foldseek
looks at its local 3D environment (the geometry between that residue and
its closest neighbour in space) and assigns one of 20 discrete
structural states, the **3Di alphabet**. A structure becomes a string of
3Di letters, one per residue, and two structures can be compared with
fast sequence-alignment machinery (the same prefilter-and-align
approach as MMseqs2) instead of expensive geometric superposition:

```
3D coordinates
   → local geometry around each residue
   → one 3Di state per residue
   → a structural "sequence"
   → fast alignment and database search
```

This makes it possible to search the hundreds of millions of structures
in the AlphaFold Database and the PDB in seconds to minutes; Foldseek is
tens of thousands of times faster than TM-align at comparable
sensitivity.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Machine-learning preview: a learned representation

Nobody designed the 20 states of Foldseek's 3Di alphabet by hand. A
machine-learning model (a variational autoencoder) was trained on pairs
of structurally aligned residues to find a compact set of recurring 3D
environments that are conserved between related structures. You do not
need to know how such a model works; the point is that a *useful
representation can itself be learned from data*. In Session 5, humans
chose the representation (amino acids) and the scoring scheme
(BLOSUM62); in Foldseek, machine learning helped choose the
representation. Sessions 7–12 build up the machinery behind models that
learn increasingly powerful representations.
:::

**A worked comparison**, run locally with Foldseek on three structures:
the two hemoglobin states used on this page (`2HHB`, deoxy; `1HHO`, oxy)
and green fluorescent protein (`1EMA`). Matching α-to-α or β-to-β chains
between `2HHB` and `1HHO`, the *same* protein in two states, gives a
TM-score of **0.98** and an RMSD of **0.7 Å**, about as similar as two
independently solved structures get. α against β globin (43% identical)
still gives a TM-score of **0.90–0.91** (RMSD 1.7–1.8 Å). Searching
`2HHB` against GFP returns **no hits**, even with a loosened significance
threshold.

## Domains, complexes and conformational states {#sec-s06-states}

### Structural domains

A **domain** is a compact, semi-independent unit of a structure, often
able to fold on its own and reused in many different proteins. Sessions
3 and 5 met domains from the *sequence* side: Pfam families, built from
profile HMMs. Structural classifications group domains by their 3D
shape, which, as the table above showed, can reveal relationships that
sequence misses.

**CATH** (Orengo et al., 1997) classifies domains in four levels: **C**lass
(mainly α, mainly β, α/β, few secondary structures), **A**rchitecture
(the overall arrangement of secondary-structure elements), **T**opology
(how they are connected: the fold), and **H**omologous superfamily
(domains with evidence of common ancestry). β-globin's domain is
`1.10.490.10`: Mainly Alpha → Orthogonal Bundle → Globin-like → Globins.
So are myoglobin, neuroglobin and the *M. tuberculosis* truncated
hemoglobin from the table above. Pfam, working from sequence, needs a
separate family for the truncated hemoglobin (PF01152, "Bacterial-like
globin", not PF00042, "Globin") and connects the two only at the level of
a *clan*. GFP, in contrast, is in CATH class 2 (Mainly Beta), Beta
Barrel.

Three other classifications exist, with different philosophies:
**SCOP** (Murzin et al., 1995; expert manual curation), **ECOD** (Cheng
et al., 2014; organized by evolutionary relationship), and **TED** (Lau,
Bordin et al., 2024; domains parsed automatically from the entire
AlphaFold Database, hundreds of millions of predicted structures). They
do not always agree on where one domain ends or how distant superfamilies
group together; knowing that several exist, and why, matters more than
picking one.

### Quaternary structure, interfaces and ligands

A complex is held together by **interfaces**: patches of surface where
two chains touch, usually more hydrophobic and more conserved than the
rest of the surface. Many proteins also bind **ligands**, small molecules
or ions such as hemoglobin's heme groups. Interfaces and ligand-binding
sites are where much of a protein's function happens, and predicting
them is one of the open problems of Session 12.

### One protein, more than one structure: hemoglobin T and R

A PDB entry is one snapshot of one state. Hemoglobin has two classic
states: deoxy (**T**, tense; `2HHB`) and oxy (**R**, relaxed; `1HHO`).
Each chain hardly changes (TM-score 0.98 between the states), but the
two α/β pairs rotate relative to each other by about 13–15° (Baldwin &
Chothia, 1979; the third discussion problem measures it). The notebook measures one consequence: the distance
between the iron atoms of the two β-chain hemes is about 5 Å shorter in
the oxy state. This quaternary change is how hemoglobin binds oxygen
cooperatively: binding at one subunit makes binding at the others easier.

So **a PDB structure is not necessarily "the" structure of a protein.**
Proteins can occupy different conformational states depending on
ligands, partners and conditions. This matters when a predicted model is
compared with "the" experimental structure, and it is one of the
limitations Session 12 returns to: AlphaFold usually predicts one state.

## From structure back to sequence prediction {#sec-s06-predict}

### Secondary structure as a prediction target

Given only the sequence, could a computer predict which residues become
helix, strand or coil? Stated as a learning problem:

```
input:   the sequence (or its profile), one window per residue
target:  H (helix), E (strand) or C (coil) for every residue
```

The training labels come from solved structures, assigned by DSSP as in
the notebook. What information could help? The residue itself (some
amino acids favour helices, others strands; proline and glycine break
both), its neighbours in the sequence, and, from Session 5, how that
position varies across homologous sequences: a profile. Sessions 7–11
develop the machinery for learning such mappings, and the course returns
to this problem in Sessions 7, 9 and 10 and in the capstone project.

### Predicting the whole fold

Predicting the full 3D structure has been one of biology's hardest
problems for decades. Since 1994 the **CASP** competition (Critical
Assessment of Structure Prediction) has tested methods blindly, on
structures that are solved but not yet published. The classical
strategies each build on something you have already met:

- **Physics** (*de novo* or *ab initio* modelling): search for the
  lowest-energy arrangement of the chain, using physical interactions.
  Rigorous in principle, but so expensive that it long worked only for
  small proteins. **Rosetta** (Baker lab) assembles structures from
  short fragments of known structures and grew into a tool for protein
  *design*.
- **Comparative (homology) modelling**: find a related protein of known
  structure (Sessions 4–5) and build the model on it as a template.
  Reliable when a template exists; useless for a new fold. The table
  above shows why it works: related sequences share their structure.
- **Evolutionary restraints**: residues that touch tend to mutate
  together, so large alignments (Session 5) reveal which pairs are in
  contact, filling in a contact map like the one above.
- **Deep learning**: AlphaFold2 (2020) combines learned representations,
  evolutionary information and geometry, and was the breakthrough in
  CASP14. David Baker, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024
  Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein design and structure prediction.
  Session 12 covers it, once Sessions 7–11 have built up the
  neural-network machinery.

The course's path from here, in representations:

```
sequence
  → profile / evolutionary information      (Session 5)
  → learned representation                  (Sessions 7–11)
  → local structure, contacts, distances    (Sessions 7, 10, 12)
  → 3D structure                            (Session 12)
```

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Homology modeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_modeling) and [CASP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CASP)
- Rosetta Commons, [`rosettacommons.org`](https://rosettacommons.org/)

## The lab

**Full lab, PyMOL first**, on three structures beyond hemoglobin: an HIV
envelope glycoprotein trimer with an antibody (`7LXM`) for
representations, chains, structural alignment (`cealign`) and finding a
sequence inside a structure; a chitinase with bound metal ions and an
inhibitor (`8C6Z`) for ligands and charged residues; and human
neuroglobin (`1OJ6`) for the central comparison, run with Foldseek in
[`notebooks/session06-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session06-lab.ipynb):

```
same protein, experimental vs. AlphaFold prediction  → nearly identical
a different globin (hemoglobin)                       → same fold
GFP                                                   → unrelated fold
```

Today AlphaFold DB simply supplies a structure to inspect; Session 12
asks how that prediction is produced and how to decide which parts of it
to trust. The lab ends with a structural domain lookup in CATH, and
shows how to view structures directly in VS Code (the Protein Viewer
extension, handy on the course server).

## What's next

This session gave you structural properties worth predicting from
sequence. Session 7 starts building the machinery: it returns to the
weighted sum a PSSM computes, $S(x) = \sum_i w[i, x_i]$, formalizes it as a
**perceptron** whose weights are *learned* from labelled examples, and
applies it to the secondary structure you met today: Rost & Sander's PHD
method, and why the helix you saw in PyMOL can be hard to predict from a
window of residues.
